text.p: State trustbusters Wednesday accused Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. of "stonewalling" and warned they will subpoena secret information if the office superstores do not let them see it voluntarily.
Several states are considering taking action against the proposed merger of the two office superstores and say they need the secret information to decide whether to go ahead.
Their actions would be in addition to a Federal Trade Commission challenge. The FTC argues that the merger would raise prices to consumers.

Federal District Court Judge Thomas Hogan signed a "protective order" Wednesday holding more than 80 boxes of evidence secret because it includes proprietary pricing information and documents involving corporate strategy.
Staples and Office Depot argued that the materials in Hogan's court should also be protected from state trustbusters, saying that if the states want information, they can subpoena it themselves.

Office Depot and Staples do "not contemplate giving (papers) to nonparties contemplating seeking entrance" to the case, Christopher Curran said before Judge Hogan. He said the states should not "be able to dally willy nilly" about what they want to see.
Curran argued that if the states wish, they should enter the case with the FTC so they will be bound by the outcome.
An FTC lawyer told Hogan that a federal-state compact permits the FTC to share materials with states. Hogan said he would consider the views of both sides and then rule.

State antitrust officials expressed impatience about the attitude of Staples and Office Depot and said they were nearly ready to go through the expensive and time-consuming process of issuing their own subpoenas.

"We in Maryland are very concerned about the stonewalling tactics being used by Staples and Office Depot to prevent the attorney general from protecting the interests of Maryland consumers," said Ellen Cooper, chief of the Maryland attorney general's antitrust section in Baltimore.
California trustbuster Kathleen Foote, supervising deputy attorney general of the antitrust section, said in San Francisco that her state has been seeking information since February.
"I am going to recommend to my front office that subpoenas issue," she said.
New York's top trustbuster, Stephen Houck, said: "If they don't have anything to hide they should give us the necessary information."
Office Depot stock rose 25 cents to $13.75 on the New York Stock Exchange, while Staples was off 25 cents at $20.375 on Nasdaq.
